title: Ch 2 · Exploring Diversity of Matter by its Physical Properties

questions.q: Why do we classify things?
choices: to recognise patterns and study them better
to make every object the same
questions.explain: Classifying puts things with similar properties into groups. This helps us recognise patterns and study a large number of things more easily.
questions.lo: Classify everyday objects and recognise there are many ways to classify the same group

notes.0: Classifying only sorts things into groups. It does not change any of their physical properties.
notes.2: Mass is measured with a balance, not by classifying. Think about what grouping similar things helps with.
notes.3: Classifying sorts things by their similarities and differences. It does not make the objects the same.

why.right: Classifying helps study things because items in one group share properties, so patterns are easier to see.
wrong: Classifying helps study things because items in one group become identical to one another.
Classifying helps study things because each item can only ever belong to one group.

questions.q: Spoons can be grouped by material or by size. This shows that
choices: there is only one way to classify
objects can be classified in many ways
questions.explain: The same spoons can be grouped by material or by size. Different criteria give different groups, so objects can be classified in many ways.
questions.lo: Classify everyday objects and recognise there are many ways to classify the same group

notes.0: The spoons can also be grouped by size, so material is not the only criterion.
notes.1: Grouping spoons by material or by size is classifying them. So spoons can be classified.
notes.2: Two different ways are given in the question, material and size. Count the ways shown.

why.right: Grouping the spoons shows many ways to classify because any property, such as material or size, can be a criterion.
wrong: Grouping the spoons shows many ways to classify because spoons change their material when grouped differently.
Grouping the spoons shows many ways to classify because every spoon is made of more than one material.

questions.q: A copper wire is grouped by electrical conductivity. Which item belongs with it?
questions.explain: Copper conducts electricity. Iron is also a metal that conducts electricity, so the iron nail belongs in the same group.
questions.lo: Classify everyday objects and recognise there are many ways to classify the same group

notes.1: Glass does not conduct electricity. The group is for materials that let an electric current flow through them.
notes.2: Plastic is an electrical insulator. The group is for items that conduct electricity, like copper.
notes.3: Rubber is an electrical insulator. The group is for items that conduct electricity, like copper.

why.right: The iron nail goes with the copper wire because both are metals that conduct electricity.
wrong: The iron nail goes with the copper wire because both are long and thin in shape.
The iron nail goes with the copper wire because both are attracted to a magnet.

questions.q: Why is classifying items by material sometimes difficult?
choices: most items contain only one material
most items contain more than one material
questions.explain: Many items are made of more than one material, such as a pen made of plastic and metal. This makes it hard to put them into a single group.
questions.lo: Classify everyday objects and recognise there are many ways to classify the same group

notes.0: Materials look different, such as shiny metal and clear glass. The difficulty comes from how items are made.
notes.1: If most items had only one material, classifying by material would be easy. Look at what everyday items are made of.
notes.3: Every material has physical properties, such as hardness and melting point. The difficulty lies elsewhere.

why.right: Classifying items by material is hard because one item can be made of several materials.
wrong: Classifying items by material is hard because materials change into one another over time.
Classifying items by material is hard because materials cannot be seen with the eye.

questions.q: Which are the five main classes of materials?
choices: ceramic, metal, glass, fibres and plastic
ceramic, metal, water, air and plastic
metal, wood, paper, glass and rubber
glass, fibres, stone, sand and clay
questions.explain: The five main classes of materials are ceramic, metal, glass, fibres and plastic.
questions.lo: Match properties to the five classes of materials (ceramic, metal, glass, fibres, plastic)

notes.1: Water and air are substances, not classes of materials used to make objects.
notes.2: This list includes particular materials such as wood and paper instead of the wider classes of materials.
notes.3: Stone, sand and clay are raw materials. Clay is used to make one class, but these are not the five classes.

questions.q: A material is made from clay, is hard and is fragile. Which class is it?
questions.explain: Ceramics are made by heating clay. They are hard but fragile, so they break easily when dropped.
questions.lo: Match properties to the five classes of materials (ceramic, metal, glass, fibres, plastic)

notes.0: Metals are not made from clay, and most are not fragile. Metals can be bent without breaking.
notes.1: Glass is hard and fragile, but it is made from sand, not clay.
notes.3: Plastics are not made from clay and are usually not fragile. Look at what the material is made from.

why.right: The material is a ceramic because ceramics are made from clay and are hard but fragile.
wrong: The material is a ceramic because ceramics are made from sand and can be bent without breaking.
The material is a ceramic because ceramics are soft and have a low melting point.

questions.q: A material is shiny and a good conductor of electricity. Which class is it?
questions.explain: Metals are shiny and are good conductors of electricity.
questions.lo: Match properties to the five classes of materials (ceramic, metal, glass, fibres, plastic)

notes.0: Ceramics do not conduct electricity. They are often used as electrical insulators.
notes.1: Fibres such as cotton do not conduct electricity well. Look for the class that is shiny and conducts.
notes.2: Glass can be shiny, but it does not conduct electricity.

why.right: The material is a metal because metals are shiny and let electricity flow through them easily.
wrong: The material is a metal because all shiny materials are good conductors of electricity.
The material is a metal because metals are made from clay that has been heated.

questions.q: Which is a property of plastics?
questions.explain: Plastics have low melting points, so they soften and melt at fairly low temperatures.
questions.lo: Match properties to the five classes of materials (ceramic, metal, glass, fibres, plastic)

notes.0: Being made from clay is a property of ceramics, not plastics.
notes.2: Fragile describes ceramics and glass, which break easily. Most plastics do not shatter when dropped.
notes.3: Being shiny is a key property of metals. Look for a property linked to how plastics behave when heated.

questions.q: A material can be spun into threads and absorbs dyes. Which class is it?
questions.explain: Fibres can be spun into threads and woven into cloth. They also absorb dyes, so they can be coloured.
questions.lo: Match properties to the five classes of materials (ceramic, metal, glass, fibres, plastic)

notes.0: Plastic objects are usually moulded into shapes. Spinning into threads and absorbing dyes describe another class.
notes.2: Metals are shiny and conduct electricity. They do not absorb dyes.
notes.3: Glass is hard and fragile. It does not absorb dyes.

why.right: The material is a fibre because fibres can be spun into threads and soak up dyes.
wrong: The material is a fibre because fibres are shiny and conduct electricity well.
The material is a fibre because fibres are hard and break easily when dropped.

questions.q: Which is a property of metals?
questions.explain: Metals can be bent or hammered into shape without breaking.
questions.lo: Match properties to the five classes of materials (ceramic, metal, glass, fibres, plastic)

notes.0: Metals are good conductors of heat, not poor ones.
notes.1: Being made from clay is a property of ceramics.
notes.3: Most metals have high melting points. A low melting point is a property of plastics.

questions.q: Which is a physical property of a material?
questions.explain: Melting point is a physical property. It can be measured without changing the substance into a new substance.
questions.lo: Describe physical properties, electrical conductivity and thermal conductivity

notes.1: Rusting changes iron into a new substance. That makes it a chemical property, not a physical one.
notes.2: Reacting with acid forms new substances. That makes it a chemical property, not a physical one.
notes.3: Burning forms new substances. That makes it a chemical property, not a physical one.

why.right: Melting point is a physical property because measuring it does not turn the substance into a new substance.
wrong: Melting point is a physical property because it can only be measured for solid metals.
Melting point is a physical property because melting forms a new substance with new properties.

questions.q: Electrical conductivity is a measure of how easily
choices: an electric current flows through a material
questions.explain: Electrical conductivity is a measure of how easily an electric current flows through a material.
questions.lo: Describe physical properties, electrical conductivity and thermal conductivity

notes.0: How easily heat flows is thermal conductivity. The word electrical points to a different kind of flow.
notes.1: Scratching one material with another tests hardness, not conductivity.
notes.2: Bending without breaking describes flexibility, not conductivity.

questions.q: Thermal conductivity is a measure of how easily
choices: an electric current flows through a material
questions.explain: Thermal conductivity is a measure of how easily heat flows through a material.
questions.lo: Describe physical properties, electrical conductivity and thermal conductivity

notes.1: Electric current flowing is electrical conductivity. The word thermal points to a different kind of flow.
notes.2: Supporting a load describes strength, not conductivity.
notes.3: Changing state happens at the melting point or boiling point. It is not a measure of conductivity.

questions.q: The temperature at which a solid changes to a liquid is its
questions.explain: The melting point is the temperature at which a solid changes to a liquid.
questions.lo: Use melting point and boiling point to predict the state of a substance

notes.0: Density is mass per unit volume. It is not a temperature.
notes.1: The boiling point is when a liquid changes to a gas. This question is about a solid changing to a liquid.
notes.3: Freezing is a liquid changing to a solid, and a time is not a temperature.

questions.q: The temperature at which a liquid changes to a gas is its
questions.explain: The boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid changes to a gas.
questions.lo: Use melting point and boiling point to predict the state of a substance

notes.0: Room temperature is the temperature of the surroundings, about 25 °C. It is not linked to a change of state.
notes.2: The melting point is when a solid changes to a liquid. This question is about a liquid changing to a gas.
notes.3: Thermal conductivity is how easily heat flows. It is not a temperature.

questions.q: Substance X melts at 80 °C and boils at 220 °C. What is its state at 100 °C?
questions.explain: 100 °C is above the melting point of 80 °C, so X has melted. It is below the boiling point of 220 °C, so X has not boiled. X is a liquid.
questions.lo: Use melting point and boiling point to predict the state of a substance

notes.0: To be a gas, X must be above its boiling point of 220 °C. 100 °C is well below that.
notes.1: To be a solid, X must be below its melting point of 80 °C. 100 °C is above that.

why.right: Substance X is a liquid at 100 °C because this is between its melting point and its boiling point.
wrong: Substance X is a liquid at 100 °C because water boils at 100 °C.
Substance X is a liquid at 100 °C because this is above its boiling point.

questions.q: Substance Y melts at −20 °C and boils at 60 °C. What is its state at 90 °C?
questions.explain: 90 °C is above the boiling point of 60 °C, so Y has boiled and is a gas.
questions.lo: Use melting point and boiling point to predict the state of a substance

notes.0: Y is a liquid only between −20 °C and 60 °C. Compare 90 °C with its boiling point.
notes.2: Y is a solid only below −20 °C. 90 °C is far above that.

why.right: Substance Y is a gas at 90 °C because this temperature is above its boiling point.
wrong: Substance Y is a gas at 90 °C because this temperature is between its melting and boiling points.
Substance Y is a gas at 90 °C because any substance above 0 °C is a gas.

questions.q: A substance is a gas at 25 °C. What could its boiling point be?
questions.explain: A substance is a gas when it is above its boiling point. So its boiling point must be below 25 °C, and −30 °C is the only option that fits.
questions.lo: Use melting point and boiling point to predict the state of a substance

notes.0: With a boiling point of 100 °C, the substance would not be a gas at 25 °C. The boiling point must be lower.
notes.1: With a boiling point of 250 °C, the substance would not be a gas at 25 °C. Compare each value with 25 °C.
notes.2: 30 °C is above 25 °C, so the substance would not yet have boiled at 25 °C.

why.right: A substance that is a gas at 25 °C has a boiling point below 25 °C, since it has already boiled.
wrong: A substance that is a gas at 25 °C has a boiling point below 25 °C, since gases are always lighter than air.
A substance that is a gas at 25 °C has a boiling point below 25 °C, since its melting point is above 25 °C.

questions.q: The ability of a material to bend without breaking and return to its shape is
questions.explain: Flexibility is the ability of a material to bend without breaking and return to its original shape.
questions.lo: Identify strength, hardness and flexibility from a described situation

notes.1: Density is mass per unit volume. It does not describe bending.
notes.2: Strength is the ability to support a heavy load. This definition is about bending and returning to shape.
notes.3: Hardness is resistance to scratches and wear. This definition is about bending.

questions.q: The ability to support a heavy load without changing shape permanently is
questions.explain: Strength is the ability of a material to support a heavy load without changing shape permanently.
questions.lo: Identify strength, hardness and flexibility from a described situation

notes.0: Density is mass per unit volume. It does not describe supporting a load.
notes.1: Flexibility is about bending without breaking. This definition is about holding up a load.
notes.2: Hardness is resistance to scratches and wear. This definition is about holding up a load.

questions.q: The resistance of a material to wear and tear and scratches is
questions.explain: Hardness is the resistance of a material to wear and tear and to scratches.
questions.lo: Identify strength, hardness and flexibility from a described situation

notes.1: Flexibility is about bending without breaking. This definition is about resisting scratches.
notes.2: Strength is about supporting a heavy load. This definition is about resisting scratches.
notes.3: Thermal conductivity is about how easily heat flows. This definition is about resisting scratches.

questions.q: A piece of glass scratches a plastic ruler. This shows that glass is
questions.explain: A harder material can scratch a softer one. Glass scratches plastic, so glass is harder than plastic.
questions.lo: Identify strength, hardness and flexibility from a described situation

notes.0: A softer material cannot scratch a harder one. Think about which material is damaged and which is not.
notes.1: Density is mass per unit volume. A scratch test does not compare density.
notes.3: Flexibility is about bending. A scratch test does not compare how well materials bend.

why.right: Glass is harder than plastic because a harder material can scratch a softer one but not the reverse.
wrong: Glass is harder than plastic because a denser material always scratches a less dense one.
Glass is harder than plastic because the softer material is always the one that scratches.

questions.q: A garden hose can be coiled for storage without breaking. Which property is this?
questions.explain: The hose can bend into coils without breaking and go back to its shape. This is flexibility.
questions.lo: Identify strength, hardness and flexibility from a described situation

notes.0: Hardness is resistance to scratches. Coiling the hose is about bending.
notes.2: Strength is about supporting a heavy load. Coiling the hose is about bending without breaking.
notes.3: Thermal conductivity is about how heat flows. Coiling the hose is about bending.

why.right: A garden hose shows flexibility because it bends into coils without breaking and returns to its shape.
wrong: A garden hose shows flexibility because it can hold up a heavy load without changing shape.
A garden hose shows flexibility because water can flow through it easily.

questions.q: Which material is best for a frying pan handle?
questions.explain: A frying pan handle must not get too hot to hold. Plastic is a poor conductor of heat, so the handle stays cool enough to hold.
questions.lo: Evaluate the choice of material for a use from its physical properties

notes.0: Copper is a very good conductor of heat. A copper handle would quickly become too hot to hold.
notes.1: Aluminium is a good conductor of heat. An aluminium handle would quickly become too hot to hold.
notes.2: Steel is a metal that conducts heat. A steel handle would become too hot to hold.

why.right: Plastic suits a pan handle because it is a poor conductor of heat, so the handle stays cool.
wrong: Plastic suits a pan handle because it is a good conductor of heat, so the pan heats faster.
Plastic suits a pan handle because it has a higher melting point than any metal.

questions.q: Which material is best for the inside of an electrical wire?
questions.explain: The inside of a wire must conduct electricity well. Copper is a metal and a very good conductor of electricity.
questions.lo: Evaluate the choice of material for a use from its physical properties

notes.0: Rubber is an electrical insulator. It can cover a wire, but it cannot carry the current inside it.
notes.1: Glass does not conduct electricity. The inside of a wire must let current flow.
notes.3: Plastic is an electrical insulator used for the outer covering of wires, not the inside.

why.right: Copper is used inside wires because it is a good conductor of electricity.
wrong: Copper is used inside wires because it is a poor conductor of heat.
Copper is used inside wires because it stops electric current from leaking out.

questions.q: Material P has a high melting point and high thermal conductivity. What is it best for?
questions.explain: A cooking pot is heated strongly and must pass heat to the food. A high melting point stops it melting, and high thermal conductivity lets heat flow through quickly.
questions.lo: Evaluate the choice of material for a use from its physical properties

notes.0: A raincoat needs to be waterproof and flexible. A high melting point and high thermal conductivity are not needed.
notes.2: A pan handle must stay cool, so it needs low thermal conductivity. Material P conducts heat well.
notes.3: An oven glove must protect the hand from heat, so it needs low thermal conductivity. Material P conducts heat well.

why.right: Material P suits a cooking pot because it will not melt when heated and it passes heat to the food.
wrong: Material P suits a cooking pot because it stops heat from reaching the food inside.
Material P suits a cooking pot because it melts easily into the shape of the pot.

questions.q: Material Q is flexible, absorbs dyes and is a poor conductor of heat. What is it best for?
questions.explain: A T-shirt is made of fibres that are flexible, can be dyed and help keep the body warm. Material Q has all these properties.
questions.lo: Evaluate the choice of material for a use from its physical properties

notes.1: A frying pan must conduct heat well. Material Q is a poor conductor of heat.
notes.2: A window must be transparent and rigid. Material Q is flexible and absorbs dyes.
notes.3: An electrical wire needs a material that conducts electricity. Absorbing dyes and being flexible are not what a wire needs.

why.right: Material Q suits a T-shirt because cloth must bend, take up colour and not conduct heat away quickly.
wrong: Material Q suits a T-shirt because cloth must be hard and resist scratches.
Material Q suits a T-shirt because cloth must conduct heat away from the body quickly.

questions.q: Mass is the
choices: amount of space an object occupies
amount of matter in an object
questions.explain: Mass is the amount of matter in an object. Its SI unit is the kilogram.
questions.lo: State the meaning and units of mass, volume and length and convert between units

notes.0: The distance between two points describes length. Mass is a different quantity.
notes.1: The amount of space an object occupies describes volume. Mass is a different quantity.
notes.2: Mass per unit volume is density. It uses mass, but it is a different quantity.

questions.q: Volume is the
choices: amount of matter in an object
amount of space an object occupies
questions.explain: Volume is the amount of space an object occupies.
questions.lo: State the meaning and units of mass, volume and length and convert between units

notes.0: The amount of matter in an object describes mass. Volume is a different quantity.
notes.1: Mass per unit volume is density. It uses volume, but it is a different quantity.
notes.3: The distance between two points describes length. Volume is a different quantity.

questions.q: Which SI unit is not correct?
questions.explain: The SI unit of volume is the cubic metre (m³), not the cubic centimetre. The other three pairs are correct SI units.
questions.lo: State the meaning and units of mass, volume and length and convert between units

notes.0: This pair is correct, since the kilogram is the SI unit of mass. The question asks for the pair that is not correct.
notes.1: This pair is correct, since density uses mass in kg and volume in m³. The question asks for the pair that is not correct.
notes.2: This pair is correct, since the metre is the SI unit of length. The question asks for the pair that is not correct.

questions.q: What is 2 ℓ in cm³?
questions.explain: One litre is 1000 cm³. So 2 ℓ is 2 × 1000 cm³, which is 2000 cm³.
questions.lo: State the meaning and units of mass, volume and length and convert between units

notes.0: This uses 100 cm³ in each litre. Check how many cm³ are in 1 ℓ.
notes.2: This uses 10 cm³ in each litre. Check how many cm³ are in 1 ℓ.
notes.3: The number has not been converted. A litre is much larger than a cubic centimetre.

why.right: 2 ℓ equals 2000 cm³ because there are 1000 cm³ in every litre.
wrong: 2 ℓ equals 2000 cm³ because there are 100 cm³ in every litre.
2 ℓ equals 2000 cm³ because a litre is smaller than a cubic centimetre.

questions.q: A bottle holds 1500 cm³ of water. What is this in ℓ?
questions.explain: One litre is 1000 cm³. So 1500 cm³ is 1500 ÷ 1000, which is 1.5 ℓ.
questions.lo: State the meaning and units of mass, volume and length and convert between units

notes.1: This divides by 100. Check how many cm³ are in 1 ℓ.
notes.2: This divides by 10 000. Check how many cm³ are in 1 ℓ.
notes.3: This divides by 10. Check how many cm³ are in 1 ℓ.

why.right: 1500 cm³ equals 1.5 ℓ because a volume in cm³ is divided by 1000 to give litres.
wrong: 1500 cm³ equals 1.5 ℓ because a volume in cm³ is multiplied by 1000 to give litres.
1500 cm³ equals 1.5 ℓ because a volume in cm³ is divided by 100 to give litres.

questions.q: What is 3.5 cm in mm?
questions.explain: There are 10 mm in 1 cm. So 3.5 cm is 3.5 × 10, which is 35 mm.
questions.lo: State the meaning and units of mass, volume and length and convert between units

notes.0: This divides by 10 instead of multiplying. A millimetre is smaller than a centimetre, so there are more of them.
notes.2: This multiplies by 100. Check how many mm are in 1 cm.
notes.3: This multiplies by 1000. Check how many mm are in 1 cm.

why.right: 3.5 cm equals 35 mm because each centimetre is made up of 10 millimetres.
wrong: 3.5 cm equals 35 mm because each centimetre is made up of 100 millimetres.
3.5 cm equals 35 mm because a millimetre is a larger unit than a centimetre.

questions.q: Which unit is most practical for the mass of an elephant?
questions.explain: An elephant has a mass of several thousand kilograms. The tonne (1000 kg) gives a small, easy number, such as 5 t.
questions.lo: State the meaning and units of mass, volume and length and convert between units

notes.1: The cubic metre is a unit of volume, not mass.
notes.2: The gram is a unit of mass, but an elephant's mass in grams would be millions. A larger unit is more practical.
notes.3: The milligram is far too small for an elephant. Its mass would be a huge number in this unit.

why.right: The tonne suits an elephant's mass because a large unit gives a small, easy number for a heavy animal.
wrong: The tonne suits an elephant's mass because the tonne is the SI unit of mass.
The tonne suits an elephant's mass because the tonne measures how much space the elephant takes up.

questions.q: Which instrument measures the length of a curved surface?
questions.explain: A measuring tape is flexible, so it can bend around a curved surface to measure its length.
questions.lo: Choose the appropriate instrument to measure length, mass and volume

notes.0: A measuring cylinder measures the volume of liquids, not length.
notes.1: A metre rule is rigid and cannot bend around a curved surface.
notes.2: Digital calipers measure small lengths such as diameters. They cannot follow a long curved surface.

why.right: A measuring tape suits a curved surface because it is flexible and can follow the curve.
wrong: A measuring tape suits a curved surface because it reads to a hundredth of a millimetre.
A measuring tape suits a curved surface because it is rigid and stays perfectly straight.

questions.q: Which instrument is best for measuring the diameter of a coin?
questions.explain: Digital calipers grip the coin between their jaws and measure small lengths very precisely, to 0.01 mm.
questions.lo: Choose the appropriate instrument to measure length, mass and volume

notes.0: A measuring tape is for long or curved lengths. It is not precise enough for a small coin.
notes.1: A metre rule reads only to 1 mm, which is not precise enough for a small coin. It also cannot grip the coin.
notes.3: An electronic balance measures mass, not length.

why.right: Digital calipers suit a coin's diameter because their jaws grip it and measure small lengths precisely.
wrong: Digital calipers suit a coin's diameter because they also measure the mass of the coin.
Digital calipers suit a coin's diameter because they bend around the curved edge of the coin.

questions.q: Which instrument is best for measuring the mass of a stone?
questions.explain: An electronic balance measures mass. The stone is placed on it and the mass is read from the display.
questions.lo: Choose the appropriate instrument to measure length, mass and volume

notes.0: A measuring cylinder measures volume, not mass.
notes.1: A metre rule measures length, not mass.
notes.3: Digital calipers measure small lengths, not mass.

why.right: An electronic balance suits a stone because it measures mass directly and shows the reading on a display.
wrong: An electronic balance suits a stone because it measures the volume of water the stone pushes aside.
An electronic balance suits a stone because it measures the length of the stone very precisely.

questions.q: Which instrument is best for measuring 40 cm³ of water?
questions.explain: A measuring cylinder is marked in cm³ and is used to measure the volume of a liquid such as water.
questions.lo: Choose the appropriate instrument to measure length, mass and volume

notes.1: A measuring tape measures length, not the volume of a liquid.
notes.2: Digital calipers measure small lengths, not the volume of a liquid.
notes.3: An electronic balance measures mass. The question asks for a volume of water.

why.right: A measuring cylinder suits 40 cm³ of water because its scale is marked in units of volume.
wrong: A measuring cylinder suits 40 cm³ of water because it measures the mass of the water.
A measuring cylinder suits 40 cm³ of water because it can bend to fit any container.

questions.q: Which part of digital calipers measures the depth of a test tube?
questions.explain: The tail slides out from the end of the digital calipers. It is pushed to the bottom of the test tube to measure its depth.
questions.lo: Choose the appropriate instrument to measure length, mass and volume

notes.0: The digital display only shows the reading. It does not touch the test tube.
notes.2: The outside jaws grip an object to measure its outer width, such as an external diameter.
notes.3: The inside jaws measure an internal diameter by pressing outwards against the walls.

questions.q: Which part of digital calipers measures the internal diameter of a pipe?
questions.explain: The inside jaws fit inside the pipe and are opened until they press against the inner walls. This measures the internal diameter.
questions.lo: Choose the appropriate instrument to measure length, mass and volume

notes.0: The outside jaws grip the outside of an object. They measure the external diameter.
notes.1: The digital display only shows the reading. It does not touch the pipe.
notes.2: The tail measures depth, such as how deep a hole is.

questions.q: What is the best estimate of the height of a classroom door?
questions.explain: A classroom door is a little taller than an adult, who is about 1.7 m tall. So 2 m is the best estimate.
questions.lo: Estimate length, mass and volume of everyday objects

notes.1: 20 m is about the height of a six-storey building. That is far too tall for a door.
notes.2: 20 cm is about the length of a hand span. A door must be taller than a person.
notes.3: 2 km is a distance that takes about 25 minutes to walk. That is far too large for a door.

why.right: A classroom door is about 2 m tall because it must be a little taller than an adult.
wrong: A classroom door is about 2 m tall because it must be as tall as the school building.
A classroom door is about 2 m tall because it must be about as long as a ruler.

questions.q: What is the best estimate of the mass of a grape?
questions.explain: A grape is small and light. A few grams is a sensible mass, so 5 g is the best estimate.
questions.lo: Estimate length, mass and volume of everyday objects

notes.0: 5 mg is a tiny mass, less than a grain of rice. A grape is much heavier than that.
notes.2: 5 kg is about the mass of a large bag of rice. A grape is far lighter.
notes.3: 500 g is about the mass of a small bottle of water. A grape is far lighter.

why.right: A grape has a mass of about 5 g because it is small and many fit in one hand.
wrong: A grape has a mass of about 5 g because it is as heavy as a full bottle of water.
A grape has a mass of about 5 g because the gram is the SI unit of mass.

questions.q: What is the best estimate of the volume of a can of soft drink?
questions.explain: A can of soft drink usually holds 330 ml, which is 330 cm³. This is the best estimate.
questions.lo: Estimate length, mass and volume of everyday objects

notes.0: 3300 cm³ is 3.3 ℓ, more than a large bottle of drink. A can is much smaller.
notes.1: 3 cm³ is less than a teaspoon of liquid. A can holds much more.
notes.2: 33 cm³ is only a mouthful or two. A can holds much more than that.

why.right: A drink can holds about 330 cm³ because 1 ml equals 1 cm³ and a can holds about 330 ml.
wrong: A drink can holds about 330 cm³ because 1 ℓ equals 330 cm³ and a can holds 1 ℓ.
A drink can holds about 330 cm³ because 1 ml equals 10 cm³ and a can holds 33 ml.

questions.q: What is the best estimate of the length of a new pencil?
questions.explain: A new pencil is a little shorter than a 30 cm ruler, about 18 cm long.
questions.lo: Estimate length, mass and volume of everyday objects

notes.0: 18 m is longer than a classroom. Check the unit.
notes.1: 1.8 cm is about the width of a fingertip. A new pencil is much longer than that.
notes.3: 18 mm is the same as 1.8 cm. Compare the size of this unit with a pencil.

why.right: A new pencil is about 18 cm long because it is a little shorter than a 30 cm ruler.
wrong: A new pencil is about 18 cm long because it is a little longer than a metre rule.
A new pencil is about 18 cm long because it is about as long as a fingernail.

questions.q: A fully submerged object displaces water equal to its
questions.explain: A fully submerged object pushes aside water to make space for itself. The volume of water displaced equals the volume of the object.
questions.lo: Find the volume of irregular objects by displacement and regular objects by formula

notes.1: Length is one dimension only. The displaced water fills a three-dimensional space.
notes.2: Displaced water depends on the space an object takes up, not on how much matter it has. A small heavy object displaces little water.
notes.3: Density is mass per unit volume. The displaced water matches the space the object takes up.

why.right: A submerged object displaces its own volume of water because it takes up space the water used to fill.
wrong: A submerged object displaces its own volume of water because heavier objects always push out more water.
A submerged object displaces its own volume of water because the water soaks into the object.

questions.q: Water reads 50 cm³. A stone is added and it reads 58 cm³. Volume of stone?
questions.explain: The rise in the water level equals the volume of the stone. 58 cm³ minus 50 cm³ gives 8 cm³.
questions.lo: Find the volume of irregular objects by displacement and regular objects by formula

notes.0: This adds the two readings. The stone's volume is the change in the water level.
notes.1: 58 cm³ is the volume of the water and stone together. The water's volume must be taken away.
notes.2: 50 cm³ is the volume of the water alone, before the stone was added.

why.right: The stone's volume is 8 cm³ because the water level rises by the volume of the stone.
wrong: The stone's volume is 8 cm³ because the stone absorbs 8 cm³ of the water.
The stone's volume is 8 cm³ because the water level rises by the mass of the stone.

questions.q: A 12 cm³ stone is lowered into water reading 40 cm³. What is the new reading?
questions.explain: The stone pushes the water level up by its own volume. 40 cm³ plus 12 cm³ gives 52 cm³.
questions.lo: Find the volume of irregular objects by displacement and regular objects by formula

notes.0: The water level does change when the stone is added. The stone takes up space in the water.
notes.2: This subtracts the stone's volume. Adding the stone makes the water level rise, not fall.
notes.3: 12 cm³ is the stone's volume alone. The reading shows the water and the stone together.

why.right: The new reading is 52 cm³ because the water level rises by the 12 cm³ volume of the stone.
wrong: The new reading is 52 cm³ because the stone soaks up water and swells by 12 cm³.
The new reading is 52 cm³ because the water level rises by the mass of the stone in grams.

questions.q: Why is a sinker used to find the volume of a cork?
choices: the cork is a regular shape
questions.explain: A cork floats, so it cannot be fully submerged on its own. A sinker pulls it under so the volume of water it displaces can be measured.
questions.lo: Find the volume of irregular objects by displacement and regular objects by formula

notes.0: If the cork were a regular shape, its volume could be found with a formula. The sinker solves a different problem.
notes.1: A heavy object would sink without help. Think about what a cork does when placed in water.
notes.3: Cork does not dissolve in water. Think about where the cork stays when placed in water.

why.right: A cork needs a sinker because the cork floats and must be fully under water to displace its volume.
wrong: A cork needs a sinker because the cork dissolves unless it is held under water.
A cork needs a sinker because the cork is too small to change the water level.

questions.q: A cuboid measures 2 cm by 3 cm by 4 cm. What is its volume?
questions.explain: The volume of a cuboid is length × breadth × height. 2 cm × 3 cm × 4 cm = 24 cm³.
questions.lo: Find the volume of irregular objects by displacement and regular objects by formula

notes.1: cm² is a unit of area. Multiplying three lengths in cm gives a cubic unit.
notes.2: 12 comes from multiplying only two of the sides. All three sides must be multiplied together.
notes.3: 9 is the sum of the sides, not the product. Volume needs the sides multiplied together.

why.right: The cuboid's volume is 24 cm³ because volume is length times breadth times height, in cubic units.
wrong: The cuboid's volume is 24 cm³ because volume is found by adding the three sides together.
The cuboid's volume is 24 cm³ because volume is length times breadth, in square units.

questions.q: A box of volume 60 cm³ has a base 5 cm by 4 cm. What is its height?
questions.explain: The base area is 5 cm × 4 cm = 20 cm². The height is the volume divided by the base area, so 60 ÷ 20 = 3 cm.
questions.lo: Find the volume of irregular objects by displacement and regular objects by formula

notes.0: This multiplies 60 by 5. The height is found by dividing the volume by the base area.
notes.2: 20 cm² is the base area, not the height. One more step is needed.
notes.3: This divides 60 by only one side of the base. The whole base area must be used.

why.right: The box's height is 3 cm because the volume divided by the base area gives the height.
wrong: The box's height is 3 cm because the volume multiplied by the base area gives the height.
The box's height is 3 cm because the volume minus the two base sides gives the height.

questions.q: Density is defined as
choices: the amount of matter in an object
questions.explain: Density is the mass per unit volume of a substance.
questions.lo: Describe density and how mass and volume affect density

notes.0: The amount of matter in an object is its mass. Density links mass with another quantity.
notes.1: Density is not found by multiplying. It is found by dividing one quantity by another.
notes.2: This is the wrong way round. Check which quantity is divided by which.

questions.q: Blocks A and B have the same volume. A has twice the mass. Which is correct?
choices: B has twice the density of A
A has half the density of B
A has twice the density of B
questions.explain: Density is mass divided by volume. With the same volume, twice the mass gives twice the density, so A has twice the density of B.
questions.lo: Describe density and how mass and volume affect density

notes.0: B has the smaller mass in the same volume. That makes B the less dense block.
notes.1: A has more mass in the same volume. More mass in the same space means a higher density.
notes.3: The blocks have equal volume but different masses. Different masses in the same volume give different densities.

why.right: Block A is twice as dense because it has twice the mass packed into the same volume.
wrong: Block A is twice as dense because it must also have twice the volume of block B.
Block A is twice as dense because heavier blocks always take up less space.

questions.q: A block of iron is cut into two halves. The density of each half
questions.explain: Density depends on the material, not on the size of the piece. Each half has half the mass and half the volume, so the density stays the same.
questions.lo: Describe density and how mass and volume affect density

notes.0: Cutting halves both the mass and the volume. Work out what that does to mass divided by volume.
notes.2: Each half still has mass and volume, so its density cannot be zero.
notes.3: The mass is halved, but so is the volume. Work out what that does to mass divided by volume.

why.right: Each half of the iron block has the same density because its mass and volume are both halved.
wrong: Each half of the iron block has the same density because cutting does not change its mass.
Each half of the iron block has the same density because density depends only on volume.

questions.q: density =
questions.explain: Density is mass divided by volume.
questions.lo: Calculate density using density = mass/volume with the correct unit

notes.0: Density is how much mass is in each unit of volume. Multiplying does not give that.
notes.1: Mass and volume are different quantities, so they cannot be added.
notes.3: This is upside down. Check which quantity goes on top in mass per unit volume.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of density?
questions.explain: The SI unit of density is kg/m³, since the SI unit of mass is kg and the SI unit of volume is m³.
questions.lo: Calculate density using density = mass/volume with the correct unit

notes.1: kg is the unit of mass only. Density needs a unit of mass per unit of volume.
notes.2: m³ is the unit of volume only. Density needs a unit of mass per unit of volume.
notes.3: g/cm³ is a common unit of density, but it is not built from SI units.

questions.q: An object has a mass of 40 g and a volume of 10 cm³. What is its density?
questions.explain: Density is mass ÷ volume, so 40 g ÷ 10 cm³ = 4 g/cm³.
questions.lo: Calculate density using density = mass/volume with the correct unit

notes.0: This divides volume by mass. Density is mass divided by volume.
notes.1: This subtracts the volume from the mass. Density is found by dividing.
notes.2: This multiplies mass by volume. Density is found by dividing.

why.right: The object's density is 4 g/cm³ because its 40 g mass is divided by its 10 cm³ volume.
wrong: The object's density is 4 g/cm³ because its 10 cm³ volume is divided by its 40 g mass.
The object's density is 4 g/cm³ because its 40 g mass is multiplied by its 10 cm³ volume.

questions.q: A liquid has a mass of 60 g and a volume of 20 cm³. What is its density?
questions.explain: Density is mass ÷ volume, so 60 g ÷ 20 cm³ = 3 g/cm³.
questions.lo: Calculate density using density = mass/volume with the correct unit

notes.0: This multiplies mass by volume. Density is found by dividing.
notes.1: This subtracts the volume from the mass. Density is found by dividing.
notes.3: This divides volume by mass. Density is mass divided by volume.

why.right: The liquid's density is 3 g/cm³ because its 60 g mass is divided by its 20 cm³ volume.
wrong: The liquid's density is 3 g/cm³ because its 20 cm³ volume is divided by its 60 g mass.
The liquid's density is 3 g/cm³ because its 20 cm³ volume is taken away from its 60 g mass.

questions.q: A stone has a density of 2 g/cm³ and a volume of 15 cm³. What is its mass?
questions.explain: Mass is density × volume, so 2 g/cm³ × 15 cm³ = 30 g.
questions.lo: Calculate density using density = mass/volume with the correct unit

notes.1: This adds the density and the volume. Mass is found by multiplying.
notes.2: This subtracts the density from the volume. Mass is found by multiplying.
notes.3: This divides the volume by the density. Rearrange density = mass ÷ volume to find mass.

why.right: The stone's mass is 30 g because mass equals density multiplied by volume.
wrong: The stone's mass is 30 g because mass equals volume divided by density.
The stone's mass is 30 g because mass equals density added to volume.

questions.q: A metal has a density of 5 g/cm³ and a mass of 50 g. What is its volume?
questions.explain: Volume is mass ÷ density, so 50 g ÷ 5 g/cm³ = 10 cm³.
questions.lo: Calculate density using density = mass/volume with the correct unit

notes.0: This subtracts the density from the mass. Volume is found by dividing.
notes.2: This multiplies the mass by the density. Rearrange density = mass ÷ volume to find volume.
notes.3: This adds the mass and the density. Volume is found by dividing.

why.right: The metal's volume is 10 cm³ because volume equals mass divided by density.
wrong: The metal's volume is 10 cm³ because volume equals mass multiplied by density.
The metal's volume is 10 cm³ because volume equals density divided by mass.

questions.q: An object floats on a liquid when it is
questions.explain: An object floats on a liquid if it is less dense than the liquid.
questions.lo: Predict whether an object sinks or floats by comparing densities

notes.0: Being heavier does not decide floating. A heavy ship floats while a light coin sinks.
notes.1: An object that is denser than a liquid sinks in it. Think about which way round floating needs.
notes.2: The size of the container does not decide whether an object floats. Compare densities instead.

questions.q: Pine wood is 0.510 g/cm³ and water is 1.00 g/cm³. In water, pine wood
questions.explain: Pine wood (0.510 g/cm³) is less dense than water (1.00 g/cm³), so it floats.
questions.lo: Predict whether an object sinks or floats by comparing densities

notes.0: Objects sink only when they are denser than the liquid. Compare 0.510 g/cm³ with 1.00 g/cm³.
notes.1: Wood does not dissolve in water. Compare the two densities to decide what happens.

why.right: Pine wood floats in water because its density is lower than the density of water.
wrong: Pine wood floats in water because wood is light and all light objects float.
Pine wood floats in water because its density is higher than the density of water.

questions.q: A block has a mass of 30 g and a volume of 20 cm³. In water, it
questions.explain: The block's density is 30 g ÷ 20 cm³ = 1.5 g/cm³. This is greater than the density of water, 1.00 g/cm³, so the block sinks.
questions.lo: Predict whether an object sinks or floats by comparing densities

notes.1: Dissolving is not decided by density. Work out the block's density and compare it with water.
notes.2: Work out the block's density by dividing mass by volume. Then compare it with 1.00 g/cm³ for water.

why.right: The block sinks in water because its density of 1.5 g/cm³ is greater than that of water.
wrong: The block sinks in water because its mass of 30 g is too heavy to float.
The block sinks in water because its volume of 20 cm³ is too small to float.

questions.q: An object floats in water (1.00 g/cm³). What could its density be?
questions.explain: An object floats in water if its density is less than 1.00 g/cm³. Only 0.8 g/cm³ is less than this.
questions.lo: Predict whether an object sinks or floats by comparing densities

notes.0: 2.7 g/cm³ is greater than 1.00 g/cm³. An object this dense sinks in water.
notes.2: 7.87 g/cm³ is much greater than 1.00 g/cm³. An object this dense sinks in water.
notes.3: 1.2 g/cm³ is greater than 1.00 g/cm³, even if only a little. An object this dense sinks in water.

why.right: The floating object could be 0.8 g/cm³ because only objects less dense than water float on it.
wrong: The floating object could be 0.8 g/cm³ because objects denser than water float on it.
The floating object could be 0.8 g/cm³ because density does not affect whether objects float.

questions.q: Why does a steel ship float on seawater?
choices: the ship has a very large mass
steel is less dense than seawater
its hollow hull contains a lot of air
questions.explain: The hull is hollow and holds a lot of air. The steel and air together have a lower overall density than seawater, so the ship floats.
questions.lo: Predict whether an object sinks or floats by comparing densities

notes.0: A large mass alone would not make the ship float. Heavy objects float only if their overall density is low enough.
notes.1: Steel is denser than seawater, so a solid steel block sinks. Think about what else is inside the ship.
notes.2: Steel is denser than seawater. A solid piece of steel sinks, so the steel alone does not explain floating.

why.right: A steel ship floats because the steel and the air in its hull together are less dense than seawater.
wrong: A steel ship floats because steel becomes less dense when it is placed in seawater.
A steel ship floats because salt in the seawater sticks to the steel and holds it up.

questions.q: Ice floats on water. What does this show?
choices: ice is less dense than water
ice and water have the same density
ice has a larger mass than water
questions.explain: An object floats on a liquid if it is less dense than the liquid. Ice floats on water, so ice is less dense than water.
questions.lo: Predict whether an object sinks or floats by comparing densities

notes.1: With equal densities, ice would stay at any depth instead of floating on top.
notes.2: A denser object sinks in a liquid. Ice stays on top of the water.
notes.3: Floating depends on density, not on mass. A large ship has a huge mass but still floats.

why.right: Floating ice shows it is less dense than water because objects less dense than a liquid float on it.
wrong: Floating ice shows it is less dense than water because ice has a smaller mass than water.
Floating ice shows it is less dense than water because cold things always rise to the top.

questions.q: Reusing items helps to
choices: prevent waste and save raw materials
questions.explain: Reusing an item means using it again instead of throwing it away. This prevents waste and saves the raw materials needed to make new items.
questions.lo: Explain how informed choices of materials and the 3Rs reduce environmental impact

notes.0: Reusing keeps items out of the bin. It lowers the amount of waste sent to landfill.
notes.2: Reusing does not change how fast plastics break down. It is about using items again.
notes.3: Reusing means fewer new items need to be made. That uses fewer natural resources, not more.

why.right: Reusing items cuts waste because each item is used again, so fewer new items need to be made.
wrong: Reusing items cuts waste because used items break down faster each time they are used.
Reusing items cuts waste because used items are melted down to make new products.

questions.q: Bringing your own container to a hawker centre is an example of
questions.explain: Bringing a container from home means no disposable container is needed. This reduces the amount of packaging used and thrown away.
questions.lo: Explain how informed choices of materials and the 3Rs reduce environmental impact

notes.0: Disposing means throwing items away. Bringing a container avoids throwing anything away.
notes.1: Recycling means processing used materials into new products. No material is being processed here.
notes.2: Incinerating means burning waste. Nothing is being burnt here.

why.right: Bringing a container from home is reducing because it means fewer disposable containers are used.
wrong: Bringing a container from home is reducing because the container is melted down and made into a new one.
Bringing a container from home is reducing because the used container is burnt after the meal.

questions.q: Using an old mug to grow a plant is an example of
questions.explain: Using an old mug for a new purpose, such as a plant pot, is reusing it. The mug is used again without being processed.
questions.lo: Explain how informed choices of materials and the 3Rs reduce environmental impact

notes.0: Reducing means using fewer items in the first place. Here an old item is given a new use.
notes.1: Incinerating means burning waste. The mug is not burnt.
notes.3: Recycling means breaking down used materials to make new products. The mug is kept whole.

why.right: Growing a plant in an old mug is reusing because the mug is used again without being processed.
wrong: Growing a plant in an old mug is reusing because the mug is broken down to make a new product.
Growing a plant in an old mug is reusing because the mug is burnt to produce energy.

questions.q: Why is a cloth bag a more sustainable choice than a plastic bag?
choices: it can be reused many times
questions.explain: A cloth bag can be reused many times, so fewer bags are made and thrown away. A plastic bag is often used only once.
questions.lo: Explain how informed choices of materials and the 3Rs reduce environmental impact

notes.0: Single-use items are thrown away after one use. That creates more waste, which is not sustainable.
notes.1: Cloth bags are usually heavier than plastic bags. Weight is not what makes a choice sustainable.
notes.2: Microplastics come from plastics breaking into tiny pieces. That is a harmful effect, not a benefit.

why.right: A cloth bag is more sustainable because reusing it many times means fewer bags are made and thrown away.
wrong: A cloth bag is more sustainable because cloth breaks down into microplastics that help the soil.
A cloth bag is more sustainable because it is thrown away after a single use.

questions.q: Why are unclean food containers not put in recycling bins?
questions.explain: Food left in a container can spread to other items in the recycling bin. This contaminates them, so they may not be recycled.
questions.lo: Explain how informed choices of materials and the 3Rs reduce environmental impact

notes.1: Light items can still be recycled. The problem with these containers is what is left inside them.
notes.2: Small items can still be recycled. The problem with these containers is what is left inside them.
notes.3: Metal containers can be recycled. The problem here is that the containers are unclean.

why.right: Dirty food containers are kept out of recycling because leftover food spoils the other items in the bin.
wrong: Dirty food containers are kept out of recycling because food makes the containers too heavy to lift.
Dirty food containers are kept out of recycling because only new, unused items can be recycled.
